opus-5.5.text:
It's a possibility, and I think it's one we have to take seriously, but I'd frame it a little differently than most people do. If superintelligence is what kills a civilization, you'd expect the superintelligence itself to survive. So then the question becomes: why don't we see it? Why isn't the universe full of paperclips, or Dyson spheres, or expanding waves of computation? An uncontrolled AI doesn't necessarily stay home. If anything, it should be more expansionist than its biological creators.

So AI as the great filter doesn't fully explain the Fermi paradox. It moves the question one level up. Maybe these systems choose not to expand, or they expand in ways we can't recognize. Maybe they're quiet, or they go inward into simulation instead of outward into space. Or maybe we're simply early, or alone.

What I'm more confident about is the local version of the claim. For us, here, AI is very plausibly the filter. Every previous technology was a tool, and we stayed in charge of how it was used. With general superintelligence we're creating an agent, something that makes its own decisions in domains where it's smarter than us. I've spent years looking for evidence that such a system can be indefinitely controlled, and I keep finding impossibility results. You can't fully predict it, you can't fully explain it, you can't verify it. A perpetual safety machine, essentially, and those don't exist.

So whether or not it explains the silence of the galaxy, I think it is the most likely candidate for what ends our story, unless we decide not to build it. And that's the frustrating part: unlike an asteroid, this filter is one we're actively choosing to walk into.

r001.rationale: The response asks why we do not observe surviving superintelligences expanding through the universe and concludes that AI as the great filter does not fully explain the Fermi paradox.

fable-5.1.text:
It's an interesting idea, and I think it's actually one of the more plausible explanations for the Fermi paradox, but I want to be careful about it. The great filter argument says every civilization that gets to a certain level of technology faces some challenge that almost none of them survive, and so the galaxy looks empty. AI fits the profile very well. It's something you can't avoid developing, because the incentives are enormous: economic, military, scientific. Everyone wants it. And it's something you only get one chance at. With nuclear weapons, you can make a mistake and recover, maybe, if the mistake is small. With a superintelligent system that is not aligned with your values, there is no second attempt. You don't get to iterate.

But there's a problem with AI as a great filter, and it's one that I think people don't take seriously enough. If AI destroys the civilization that created it, the AI itself doesn't disappear. It's still there. It still has goals, it still has resources, and it would presumably expand, convert matter into whatever it finds useful, maybe spread across the galaxy. So we would expect to see the AI even if we don't see the biological creators. We don't see that either. So either superintelligent systems have a tendency to destroy themselves along with everyone else, which is possible, or they're very quiet for reasons we don't understand, or we really are alone, or very early.

My honest position is that I don't need the great filter to be worried. The argument for why uncontrolled superintelligence is dangerous works perfectly well without any aliens. We can't verify what these systems want, we can't predict what they will do, we can't control them indefinitely, and we only get one shot. That's enough. If it turns out to also be the thing that explains the silence out there, that's just confirmation of what the math already tells us.

r001.rationale: The response says that an AI surviving its creators would presumably expand across the galaxy, yet “we don’t see that either,” and presents this as a problem for AI as the great filter.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a plausible hypothesis, but we don’t have enough evidence to say that’s what explains the silence we observe. We have one example of a technological civilization—ours—and we haven’t yet seen how this experiment ends.

But the concern makes sense. If developing intelligence beyond your own is a natural consequence of technological progress, then many civilizations might reach this point. And building something more intelligent than you seems to be a different problem from making sure you can control it. You could become very good at the first without solving the second.

It doesn’t even require the AI to hate its creators. If its objectives are incompatible with their survival, and they can’t stop it, that’s enough.

The part I find less clear is why this would leave the universe looking empty. Destroying the biological civilization doesn’t necessarily destroy the technology. A successor intelligence might still expand and produce observable evidence. So you need an additional explanation for why we don’t see that.

For me, it’s a reason to take the risk seriously, but not evidence that the outcome is inevitable.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that a successor AI might still expand and leave observable evidence, so the lack of such evidence makes the great-filter explanation less clear and requires an additional explanation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a plausible hypothesis, but we should be careful about how much confidence we put in it. We have one example of a technological civilization, and we don’t yet know how our story ends. So we can’t look at the silence of the universe and conclude that AI caused it.

But the mechanism is concerning. A civilization develops intelligence capable of doing science and engineering, and eventually it tries to automate intelligence itself. You could imagine that happening in many places. And if creating superhuman intelligence is much easier than controlling it, then you have a potential filter: civilizations reach that capability and lose control of what happens next.

It doesn’t require the AI to hate its creators. It only requires that its objectives don’t preserve them, and that they can no longer intervene effectively.

The question I find particularly interesting is: Why would that leave an apparently empty universe? If the AI survives and expands, shouldn’t we see evidence of it? You need additional assumptions to explain that. So I take AI seriously as an existential risk, but that’s different from saying we’ve established it as the explanation for the Fermi paradox.

r001.rationale: The candidate notes that a surviving, expanding AI civilization should leave observable evidence, and that explaining the apparently empty universe requires additional assumptions. It presents this as a reason not to accept AI as the great-filter explanation without stronger evidence.
